title: Topic Management and Cohesion
welcome_lead: Beyond turns and pairs — how do speakers steer topics and stitch utterances into a coherent fabric?
meta_desc: Topic management, cohesion and coherence as A-Level discourse analysis tools.
final_note: You have mastered the textile of talk — topic threads and cohesive stitches that make discourse hold together.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In casual conversation, topic management is collaborative. In institutional talk it is often controlled — a doctor opens with so how can I help? and closes with I'll see you in two weeks.

Tracking who introduces and changes topic reveals power.

Halliday and Hasan's Cohesion in English (1976) identified five cohesive devices: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical cohesion.

A short paragraph may stitch its sentences with this (reference), did so (substitution), and a thematic vocabulary (lexical cohesion).

Coherence is what readers reconstruct. Two sentences may lack obvious cohesive ties yet still hang together because we infer the link: It was raining. We took the bus.

Discourse analysis distinguishes the surface ties (cohesion) from the deeper logic (coherence).

mcqs.q: What is an adjacency pair in conversation analysis?
options: A two-part sequence where the first part conditions the second — question/answer, greeting/greeting, request/acceptance-or-refusal. The second part is 'conditionally relevant' on the first.
A semantic field is a field of study like physics or biology.
Adjacency pairs are two people who sit next to each other while talking.
Adjacency pairs are pairs of synonyms in vocabulary lists.

mcqs.q: Are features of spoken language like 'um' and 'you know' signs of poor speech?
options: Spoken language has no rules unlike written language.
No — they are functional discourse markers and planning devices that help interaction flow, manage turn-taking and signal speaker meaning.
Adjacency pairs are pairs of synonyms in vocabulary lists.
Fillers and false starts show the speaker is uneducated.
